groups.question: Can printed tools work at all?

items.text: printed a PLA Army-Navy retractor that held 13.6 kg of force before breaking. It used $0.46 of plastic.
found that their best printed retractor took more than 15 times the force that surgeons called clinically excessive.
found that autoclaving reduced a PLA retractor's failure load from 95 N to 15.7 N.
found that steam at 121 °C badly deformed PLA templates, even though it eliminated every microorganism tested.
found that a third of their chemical treatments raised the median sample weight by up to 8.3%, while the samples with the best surface quality gained nothing.
showed that 70% isopropyl alcohol removed applied bacteria from PLA without major surface changes. So alcohol looks gentler than heat.

groups.question: How people have tried to fix it

items.text: found that bacteria attached to both standard PLA and a nano-copper "antimicrobial" PLA. The copper slowed only one of the three species tested.
pushed epoxy into printed polypropylene parts, which reduced micro-voids and surface irregularities.
brushed Smooth-On XTC-3D onto printed ABS and found lower moisture uptake with little change in tensile strength. The coating began separating at a relatively low strain.
put a water-repelling coating on printed ABS and saw less water retention.

gap.label: The gap
gap.question: The gap
gap.statement: Prior research has established that printed PLA tolerates chemical disinfection and that coatings reduce absorption in other printed plastics, but none of the reviewed studies tested whether a coating on printed PLA keeps working through repeated disinfection.
gap.tableCaption: The closest studies each cover part of the question.
after: It is hypothesized that sealing will reduce liquid absorption and that repeated alcohol exposure will change how much protection the seal provides. Because evidence on repeated alcohol exposure is limited, no direction is predicted for strength, mass, or dimensions.

If a single coating step proves durable, groups printing reusable instruments in low-resource settings would gain an inexpensive way to limit disinfectant retention; if it fails, they would know not to rely on it.
